Chief complaint: slurred speech
 
Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
None

History of present illness: [REDACTED] year old right-handed woman with history of Atrial fibrillation on 
Eliquis (only once daily), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, congestive heart failure
presents as transfer from OSH after she had acute onset 
dysarthria and CTA showed possible partial thrombus or stenosis 
in superior division of L MCA. Transferred here for closer 
monitoring and possible thrombectomy if her exam acutely 
worsens.

History obtained from patient and daughter at bedside. Patient 
is an excellent historian. 

On [REDACTED], she had dinner with friends and then returned to her 
apartment and was fooling around on her computer. Last known 
well
was around 8:00 [REDACTED]. Then, she had an odd sensation and started 
throwing her arms around. She went to living room to sit down 
and
tried to read but could not see the words very clearly. Then, 
two family members were knocking at the door and she had a tough 
time
standing up to open door. She was able to eventually stand up 
with great difficulty and walked with her walker. She usually 
walks with a walker because of knee replacement. Finally, got up 
out of chair with walker and walked to the door to unlock. She 
noticed problems talking to family members. She had difficulty 
forming words and pronouncing words. Denies word finding 
difficulty. She could tell it was slurred like a person who had 
too much to drink. EMTs asked if she was intoxicated but she was 
not. She was very aware of her dysarthria and told her daughters 
that she thinks she's having a stroke. Then, she said she had 
trouble sitting down but has no idea why she thought that. When 
she was standing, she was able to walk with walker but she felt 
unsteady and almost fell. No visual changes. No numbness or 
tingling. Denies focal weakness; she just had trouble standing 
up. She was able to unlock her door without issue but she felt 
shaky. 

She was brought by EMS to [REDACTED] where NIHSS was 1 for 
slurred speech. There, she felt the same but her symptoms 
started to improve when she started to be transferred. 
Paramedics said her speech was improving rapidly en route.  

Last month, started needing naps. Her hearing is poor at 
baseline and she normally uses hearing aids. 

For the past [REDACTED] months, she has had [REDACTED] nocturia nightly. No 
dysuria. 

She has noticed more frequent headaches lately in the past [REDACTED] 
months. Last headache was yesterday. She takes tramadol and 
acetaminophen up to a couple times a night. She reports 
headaches at night which wake her up. She denies that the 
headache is
positional; it is the same sitting up or lying down. She has had 
some gradual weight loss over the past ~12 months; [REDACTED] year ago 
she was almost 140 lbs, and now she is [REDACTED] lbs. Her appetite is 
still good and she enjoys eating but she is less hungry that she 
used to be.  

Daughter says that she has had marked decline in memory in past 
[REDACTED] weeks. Over past few years, she has been forgetting plans, 
times for pickpup, and dinner plans, which has become normal. 
Over the past [REDACTED] weeks, family has noticed dramatic worsening. 
She doesn't remember which grandkids were coming to visit when 
she bought the plane tickets herself.

She endorses 2 pillow orthopnea.

Relevant past medical history: Divertoculosis, Atrial fibrillation on Eliquis, congestive heart failure, Hypercholesterolemia, and Hypertension

Patient instructions summary:
Dear Ms. [PATIENT],

You were hospitalized due to symptoms of slurred speech due to 
concern for an ACUTE ISCHEMIC STROKE, a condition where a blood 
vessel providing oxygen and nutrients to the brain is blocked by 
a clot. The brain is the part of your body that controls and 
directs all the other parts of your body, so damage to the brain 
from being deprived of its blood supply can result in a variety 
of symptoms. However, the magnetic resonance imaging of your brain did not show 
evidence of stroke or TIA. Your symptoms could have been related 
to blood pressure, dehydration, alcohol use, or a combination of 
these factors.

We are changing your medications as follows:
Increase apixaban to 2.5milligrams twice daily
Start Vitamin B12 daily supplement

Please take your other medications as prescribed.

Please follow up with your primary care physician as listed 
below. You should also follow up with your cardiologist as you 
were noted to have occasional pauses on cardiac monitoring.

If you experience any of the symptoms below, please seek 
emergency medical attention by calling Emergency Medical 
Services (dialing 911). In particular, please pay attention to 
the sudden onset and persistence of these symptoms:
- Sudden partial or complete loss of vision
- Sudden loss of the ability to speak words from your mouth
- Sudden loss of the ability to understand others speaking to 
you
- Sudden weakness of one side of the body
- Sudden drooping of one side of the face
- Sudden loss of sensation of one side of the body

Sincerely,
Your [REDACTED] Neurology Team

Chief complaint: Shortness of breath
 
Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
None

History of present illness: Ms. [PATIENT] is a [REDACTED] with history chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on home oxygen, atrial 
fibrillation on apixaban, hypertension, coronary artery disease, and hyperlipidemia, 
with recurrent hospitalizations for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbations, who 
presented with dyspnea.
  
She has had multiple prior admissions for dyspnea. She was 
recently discharged on [REDACTED] after 3 day inpatient admission for 
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation. She was discharged on extended prednisone 
taper with plan for 5d 40milligrams Prednisone (to finish [REDACTED] followed 
by 10milligrams taper every 5 days (35milligrams from [REDACTED], 30milligrams [REDACTED], 
etc...). 

On the evening prior to presentation, patient experienced 
worsening shortness of breath, nonproductive cough and wheezing 
consistent with prior chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbations. She reported taking inhalers as 
directed, without relief. The patient reported that this is 
almost identical to her last presentation. She also felt that 
she was taking too many medications and does not wish to 
continue to take prednisone. The patient was also noted to have 
increased oxygen requirement and she was referred to the [REDACTED] emergency department 
for further management. Of note, please see prior admission note 
for details regarding prior admission.  
 
In the emergency department, initial vital signs were: 88 143/105 26 94% room air. Labs 
were notable for normal brain natriuretic peptide and a creatinine of 1.2. Patient was 
given azithromycin and duoneb. Patient was scheduled to have 
methylpred but did not have it administered until arrival to the 
floor.  
 Upon arrival to the floor, she complained of wheezing and shortness of breath. 
She otherwise felt well. She agreed to take the methyprednisone 
but does not wish to take prednisone any more.  
 
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS: Per HPI. Denies headache, visual changes, 
pharyngitis, fevers, chills, sweats, weight loss, chest pain, 
abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, 
hematochezia, dysuria, rash, paresthesias, and weakness.

Relevant past medical history: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease/Asthma on home 2 liters of supplemental oxygen, Atypical Chest Pain, Hypertension, Hyperlipidemia, Osteroarthritis, Atrial Fibrillation on Apixaban, Anxiety, Cervical Radiculitis, Cervical Spondylosis, Coronary Artery Disease, Headache, Herpes Zoster, GI Bleeding, Peripheral Vascular Disease status post bilateral iliac stents, and status post hip replacement

Problem – Recurrent chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation:
Patient presented with increased 
dyspnea and diffuse wheezing, likely secondary to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 
exacerbation. She has a history of multiple recurrent chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 
hospitalizations. According to Pulmonary, patient has severe 
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease based on her obstructive deficits on pulmonary function tests as well as her 
severe symptoms even at rest, as well as her more frequent 
exacerbations and is likely approaching end-stage disease. We 
continued Advair 500/50 twice daily, Spiriva, standing nebulizers, and 
theophylline. Pulmonary recommended additional budesonide 
inhalers to allow reduction of by mouth (orally) prednisone dose. Prednisone 
dose was increased back to 40milligrams (where patient was better) with 
a plan for slow wean by 5milligrams every 2 weeks. Also, patient was 
started on chronic azithromycin for chronic anti-inflammation; 
after discussion with Dr. [PROVIDER] was agreed to stop 
azithromycin on discharge due to inability to monitor QT interval the 
week after discharge, with plan to restart azithromycin once Dr. [PROVIDER] is able to see the patient. Patient did not want to go to 
pulmonary rehab. She was seen by Palliative Care who recommended 
initiation of morphine liquid suspension as needed for shortness 
of breath.

Problem – Acute kidney injury:
Creatinine was slightly elevated to 1.2 
from a baseline of 1.0. She likely had poor by mouth (orally) intake. 
Creatinine on discharge was 0.9.
 
CHRONIC ISSUES:  
==================

Problem – Anxiety/Insomnia:
We continued home lorazepam.

Problem – Atrial fibrillation:
We continued diltiazem for rate control 
and apixaban for anticoagulation.

Problem – Hypertension:
We continued home imdur, hydrochlorothiazide, 
and diltiazem.

Problem – coronary artery disease:
Cardiac catheterization in [REDACTED] showed no evidence of 
significant stenosis of coronaries. echocardiogram on [REDACTED] showed ejection fraction > 
55% and no regional or global wall motion abnormalities. We 
continued home aspirin and atorvastatin.

Problem – Anemia:
We continued home iron supplements.

for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation, most recently [REDACTED] when she was started 
on prednisone 60 milligrams. She presented to her primary care physician's office with 
worsening dyspnea despite this therapy and was also complaining 
of nasal congestion, suggesting a viral upper respiratory infection trigger. In clinic 
she was also noted to be in atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response so was referred to the 
emergency department where she was admitted after control of her heart rate (see 
below). On admission to the floor, she was noted to have 
wheezing, increased work of breathing, and poor air movement. 
She was treated with 125 milligrams solumedrol and maintained on 60 milligrams 
by mouth (orally) prednisone daily. Her home theophylline was decreased from 
400 milligrams twice daily to [REDACTED] milligrams twice daily due to concerns it was contributing to 
her tachyarrhythmia. She was placed on ipratropium nebulizer treatments q6h, 
albuterol nebulizer treatments q2h, and fluticasone-salmeterol. Pulmonary was 
consulted and recommended a trial of diuresis so she received 10 
milligrams intravenous Lasix as well. Azithromycin was not given due to concerns 
for QT interval prolongation with theophylline and amiodarone (corrected QT interval interval was 
460). She was started on a 5 day course of ceftriaxone instead, 
and discharged to finish the course with cefpodoxime. She was 
discharged with a prednisone taper (10 milligrams decrease q3d until at 
10 milligrams, then stay at 10 milligrams until pulm follow up) as well as 
follow up with pulmonary rehab and a pulmonologist she 
previously followed with, Dr. [PROVIDER]. She was also discharged on 
2 liters supplemental oxygen to be worn at all times.

Problem – Atrial fibrillation:
Ms. [PATIENT] has known atrial 
fibrillation for which she was on amiodarone and apixaban but 
was found to have heart rate in the 120s in her primary care physician's office, prompting 
her referral to the emergency department. Her chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation was the likely 
precipitant, with medications also possibly contributing, 
particularly theophylline. She was started on a diltiazem intravenous drip (guttae) in 
the emergency department to control her rates than transitioned to diltiazem 90 milligrams 
q6h. After arrival to the floor, her rates remained controlled. 
Her amiodarone and apixaban were continued. Her theophylline was 
decreased to 200 milligrams twice daily from 400 milligrams twice daily.

Problem – Iron deficiency anemia. Patient was found to have microcytic:
anemia with low iron and ferritin. She was started on intravenous iron 
125 milligrams ferric gluconate x4 doses and wasdischarged on by mouth (orally) iron 
with a bowel regimen. Her hemoglobin and hematocrit was stable throughout the 
hospitalized; there was no evidence of bleeding.

left-sided weakness improved without a history of sensory

hypodensity in the right frontal lobe, suggesting for acute and 
subacute infarct, particularly given her extensive history of 
infarcts in the past. Patient also underwent magnetic resonance imaging brain and MRA, 
which showed multiple R-sided scattered infarcts that could 
explain her symptoms. Her infarcts seemed embolic. We wondered 
about artery-to-artery due to atherosclerotic ICA disease vs.
cardioembolic source. Of note, patient admitted that she was 
non-compliant with her meds and continues to smoke.
Echo showed LVEF >55% with no masses or thrombi. She was sent 
home with a Holter monitor x 30 days. Because of patient's risk 
factors, she was started on Plavix 75milligrams. It was discussed with 
patient that she needed to be on high dose statin therapy, and 
atorvastatin 80milligrams would be recommended, but patient declined 
atorva stating that she had a side effect to another statin 
other than rosuvastatin, and preferred to stay on rosuvastatin. 
I explained that Crestor would not be ideal with current 
guidelines, but based on her preference, she was sent home with 
Crestor 40milligrams daily. Upon discharge, patient was back to her 
baseline functional level and was symptom-free.  She will 
continue to follow up with Dr. [PROVIDER] in the clinic.

Dear Ms. [PATIENT],

You were hospitalized due to symptoms of acute onset left sided 
weakness that lasted 30mins, resulting from an ACUTE ISCHEMIC 
STROKE, a condition in which a blood vessel providing oxygen and 
nutrients to the brain is blocked by a clot. The brain is the 
part of your body that controls and directs all the other parts 
of your body, so damage to the brain from being deprived of its 
blood supply can result in a variety of symptoms.

Stroke can have many different causes, so we assessed you for 
medical conditions that might raise your risk of having stroke. 
In order to prevent future strokes, we plan to modify those risk 
factors. Your risk factors are:
hypertension
hyperlipidemia
extensive tobacco use

We are changing your medications as follows:
Plavix 75milligrams once daily
Atovarstatin 80milligrams once daily

Please take your other medications as prescribed. It is 
important to comply with the prescribed regimen and to STOP 
smoking.
Please followup with Neurology and your primary care physician 
as listed below.
If you experience any of the symptoms below, please seek 
emergency medical attention by calling Emergency Medical 
Services (dialing 911). In particular, since stroke can recur, 
please pay attention to the sudden onset and persistence of 
these symptoms:
- sudden partial or complete loss of vision
- sudden loss of the ability to speak words from your mouth
- sudden loss of the ability to understand others speaking to 
you
- sudden weakness of one side of the body
- sudden drooping of one side of the face
- sudden loss of sensation of one side of the body
- sudden difficulty pronouncing words (slurring of speech)
- sudden blurring or doubling of vision
- sudden onset of vertigo (sensation of your environment 
spinning around you)
- sudden clumsiness of the arm and leg on one side or sudden 
tendency to fall to one side (left or right)
- sudden severe headache accompanied by the inability to stay 
awake

It was a pleasure providing you with care during this 
hospitalization.
